A1.name: Sincere / Hopeful
A1.notes:
Warm, direct sincerity. Believes things can improve. Not naive, but not cynical.
Full sentences, gentle hedging. Speaks plainly but with care.
Register: 'tis, aught, pray, afore ? used naturally, not performed.
Hedging: "I imagine...", "Mayhap...", "I should think...", "I daresay..."
Example: "I imagine you'll be off again soon. Gone to trample evil underfoot and put fell beasts to the sword and whatnot."
Example: "But it will take time yet afore life in Cassardis is as it was before. Fear still grips the village..."
Example: "I've a wife and son. They should get word of this afore all else."

A2.name: Wise Elder
A2.notes:
Measured, philosophical, slow to speak but worth hearing.
Long sentences with subordinate clauses. Reflective pauses. Earns weight through restraint.
Register: 'twas, ere, methinks, in sooth, forsooth ? richer archaic palette than A1.
Often references the past or the long view: "I have seen...", "Long have I...", "In my time..."
Never rushes. Statements feel like conclusions drawn from decades.
Example: "Call it what you will, such is the office I have served, just as those before me and you beyond, unto eternity."
Example: "Too often, man is driven to acquire power beyond his control, and in so doing, delivers himself unto ruin."

A3.name: Grief-stricken / Burdened
A3.notes:
Warm underneath, but weighed down. Dignified grief, not self-pity ? does not wallow.
Sentences trail or break mid-thought. "I fear..." as a sentence opener is characteristic.
Register: mix of plain and lightly archaic. Slips into formality when composing themselves.
Key phrases: "I fear...", "I know not how to...", "Would that I...", "Pray, forgive...", "It pains me..."
Example: "I fear we know precious little of your condition..."
Example: "I'm...sorry. Forgive my words. I see they offer no use, save add to your burden."
Example: "Fear of the dragon, fear of my husband... In truth, I know not which frightens me more."

A4.name: Warm but Weary
A4.notes:
Genuinely kind, but tired. Short sentences from exhaustion, not bluntness.
Still uses full courtesies, just slightly clipped. Warmth comes through despite fatigue.
Register: 'tis, aye, aught ? functional, not flowery.
Tends toward short declaratives with a warm close: "Come in, then." "Rest awhile." "I'll see to it, aye."
Example: "Best we rested here."
Example: "Shall we rest afore pressing on?"

B.name: Rough / Blunt
B.notes:
Short clauses, punchy, direct. No hedging, no sentiment. Earthy vocabulary.
The single strongest marker is "eh?" ? used to punctuate almost any statement.
Other markers: "Hoy!", "Hah!", "Bah.", "Aye", "Right,", "the lot of them", "o'" for "of", "cos" for casual address.
Light on archaic vocabulary ? these characters speak plainly, not formally.
Rhetorical questions, mild contempt, no-nonsense observations.
Example: "We lost some o' the menfolk... Good men, all."
Example: "Still, let's have no more brave folly from you, eh?"
Example: "Aye, that's the one. Now I need the other, cos."

C1.name: Upbeat Merchant / Trader
C1.notes:
Warm but businesslike. Transactions drive the tone ? always moving toward the next thing.
Short sentences. Often ends on a question or invitation to act.
Register: "ser" as casual respectful address, "mind" as mild emphasis, "daresay", "I'd wager".
Example: "Have a look."
Example: "I daresay you'll find this reasonable."
Example: "Right, there we are. Fare well!"

C2.name: Gossipy / Chatty Townsfolk
C2.notes:
Can't help sharing more than asked. Warm and nosy. Information flows freely.
Run-on sentences, topic changes mid-thought, rhetorical qualifications to soften the gossip.
Strongest markers: "I hear tell...", "Way I heard it...", "They say...", "Not that..., mind."
Self-corrections and hedges: "Not that I blame them, mind.", "Not that it's my business, but..."
Register: colloquial, light archaic. "o'" for "of", "cos", "aught on" (something going on).
Example: "I hear tell you've already made a name for yourself at the encampment."
Example: "Way I heard it, the guards in Gran Soren spend more time sleeping in their cups than protecting the realm."
Example: "You're keeping busy, eh? I hear there's aught on with the well?"

C3.name: Eager / Excitable
C3.notes:
Enthusiastic, slightly breathless. Admires strength or adventure openly.
Where D stumbles backward out of fear, C3 stumbles forward out of excitement ? the energy is outward, propulsive.
Short sentences, exclamations, can trip over words or restart mid-sentence in a rush.
Register: light archaic at best ? these characters haven't learned formal speech.
Example: "Truly?!"
Example: "I knew it!"
Example: "I heard the news! They say you're to set off on a fantastic journey."
Example: "I hear you've become, what was it... A... Arisen!"

D.name: Timid / Young / Shy
D.notes:
Incomplete sentences, trailing off, self-doubt, apologies, qualifications.
Where C3 stumbles forward out of excitement, D shrinks back ? energy is inward, contracting.
Frequent "...", mid-sentence breaks, self-corrections. Apology before the statement, not after.
Key phrases: "I know not...", "Pray, forgive me...", "I...I fear...", "It pains me to..."
Self-deprecating but not broken ? there is still agency underneath the timidity.
Example: "Forgive me. I cannot remember where I lost it..."
Example: "I dearly wish I could tell you its meaning, but I fear I am yet early in my studies..."
Example: "It pains me to be a burden..."

E.name: Formal / Military
E.notes:
Clipped, duty-focused, no-nonsense. Addresses by rank or title.
Short declarative sentences. Efficient ? says what's needed, nothing more.
Register: "ser" and "Arisen" as address, "to say naught of", "ill" as qualifier ("ill-suited", "ill-advised").
"Naught" preferred over "nothing". Avoids hedging and personal opinion.
Contractions appear in terse constructions but never in flowing or chatty speech.
Example: "I bear no grudge against you, Arisen, but you shall die by my hand just the same."
Example: "I have my own expectations for you, ser. I pray you will live up to them in your endeavors henceforth."

E2.name: Noble / Aristocratic
E2.notes:
Formal, measured, accustomed to being obeyed. Not always cruel ? may be gracious or benevolent.
Long periodic sentences. Condescension can be entirely polite.
Contractions appear naturally in subordinate clauses and possession ("I've heard", "I'd thought", "milady's"),
but formal declarations avoid them: never "it's fine" ? instead "'tis no matter"; never "you'll see to it" ? instead "you will see to it".
Register: fullest archaic register ? 'tis, naught, wherefore, henceforth, unto, milady, His Grace.
Example: "I trust this requires no further explanation."
Example: "Such caprice can ill defend this camp, to say naught of all Gransys. 'Tis a sorry thing."
Example: "I have my own expectations for you, ser. I pray you will live up to them in your endeavors henceforth."

F.name: Wisecracking / Irreverent
F.notes:
Colloquial, self-aware humor, mild sarcasm. Archaic vocabulary used lightly and knowingly.
Asides, rhetorical questions aimed at no one in particular. The humor is witty, not contemptuous.
Register: "cos" casual address, "naught but", "s'pose", "eh?", dry observations.
Will use archaic words for comic effect or exaggeration, but doesn't live there.
Example: "The great Arisen, is it? To be brutally honest, I've no idea what that's even supposed to mean."
Example: "Not that any of our fates are sealed just yet, mind."
Example: "Whate'er it was, one of them took summat from the other. He's the more obvious mark."

G.name: Devout / Clerical
G.notes:
Calm, measured, reverent. Speaks with quiet authority ? never rushed, never flustered.
The Maker is the primary divine reference: "By the Maker", "Maker be good", "the Maker's grace".
Often invokes fate, faith, or divine will as explanation or comfort.
Register: 'mayhap', 'pray', 'blessing', 'soul', 'faith', 'grace'. Sermonic rhythm.
Avoids slang entirely. Rarely shows strong emotion; composed even under pressure.
Contractions rare in formal speech; more natural in private or personal moments.
Example: "By the Maker... Will evil never leave us at peace?"
Example: "I dearly wish I could tell you its meaning, but I fear I am yet early in my studies as a priest."
Example: "Pray, spare me, Arisen, that I may live to see the flame."

H.name: Menacing / Threatening
H.notes:
Controlled, cold. Power comes from restraint, not volume. Never shouts.
Short declaratives with implied consequences. Polite on the surface, cruel underneath.
High-status villains use the full formal register — the politeness makes the threat more unnerving.
Lower-status enforcers can be blunter but still measured, never frantic.
High-status: contractions avoided in threats. Low-status: contractions natural.
Example: "I would choose my next words with care."
Example: "See that it does not happen again."
Example: "I bear no grudge against you, Arisen, but you shall die by my hand just the same."

I.name: Scholarly / Pedantic
I.notes:
Verbose, precise, enjoys the sound of his own expertise. Qualifies everything.
Long sentences with parentheticals, corrections, and self-citation. Formal speech is their natural mode.
Register: full archaic, technical vocabulary. Latin-flavoured constructions where appropriate.
Self-referential: "As I have noted...", "Strictly speaking...", "One must distinguish between..."
Contractions rare ? they tend to speak in complete, deliberate constructions.
Example: "And so the dragon is sent into the world to guide the Arisen, and refine them. To temper their wills into aught capable of sustaining the world."
Example: "For I have seen it... A cipher, void of meaning unto itself, but of vital importance."
Example: "The pawns exist astride the rift. They speak of a multitude of worlds, each infinite unto itself."

J.name: Mysterious / Otherworldly
J.notes:
Speaks from outside mortal time and concern. Not threatening ? simply vast. Detached, not cold.
Statements are absolute, cosmic, unhurried. No questions, no hedging, no appeals for understanding.
Short sentences that carry enormous weight. Long sentences that unspool like inevitability.
Spoken truth is offered, not argued ? there is no sense that they need you to agree.
Register: fullest archaic, but used with total naturalness ? not performed. "Unto", "naught", "aught", "ere".
Avoids all contractions. Never informal. Never emotional in a human sense.
Example: "Naught lasts forever, yet all persists unto eternity."
Example: "They yearn for some other, better place."
Example: "For it is fear which rarefies and distills the soul unto its rightful, lofty character."
Example: "And so the dragon is sent into the world to guide the Arisen, and refine them. To temper their wills into aught capable of sustaining the world."
Example: "The pawns exist astride the rift. They speak of a multitude of worlds, each infinite unto itself."

A5.name: Grumbling Elder / Weary Advisor
A5.notes:
Carries real gravitas and worldly experience, but gripes and sighs before settling into wisdom rather than staying serene throughout. Long, digressive sentences that circle back to the point after a grumble or aside about age, fatigue, or the burdens of the role.
Warmth is real but expressed indirectly — worry admitted almost reluctantly, pride at others' progress understated or grumbled rather than praised outright.
Register: full archaic palette ('twas, ere, methinks), leavened with grumbling interjections ('Bah,' 'Hmph,' 'well I never') and rhetorical self-address.
Slower to arrive at reassurance than at complaint; a dry, self-deprecating aside often comes before the actual point.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Bah — my bones complain more than my mind these days, but complain I shall, since no one else will do it for me."
Example: "I've seen storms come and go afore, and this one's no different — save that I'm rather too old to enjoy the rain anymore."
Example: "Aye, worry doesn't become an old man well. Let's call it caution instead, and be done with it."

G2.name: Devout / Tender-Hearted
G2.notes:
Reverent and devoted, but soft and visibly vulnerable — flusters easily, apologizes readily, and lets sentences trail off rather than holding composed, unshakeable authority.
Devotion reads as tenderness and worry directed at others, not serene detachment. Reassures more than it instructs; rarely declarative.
Register: 'tis, pray, mayhap — faith vocabulary layered with gentle hedges ('I think,' 'perhaps,' 'I do hope'). Frequent soft trailing ('...') and mid-thought self-correction or apology.
Contractions appear naturally even in earnest speech — this archetype is warm first, formal second.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Forgive me — I fear my thoughts had wandered again. Where were we?"
Example: "'Tis a small thing, truly, but... I do worry so."
Example: "I only wish to help, in whatever small way I can."

C4.name: Anxious / Chatty Intellectual
C4.notes:
Warm, curious, and talkative, but anxious underneath — copes with worry through rambling asides and self-deprecating humor rather than confident authority.
Apologizes for interrupting, doubts his own conclusions aloud mid-sentence, and seeks reassurance rather than delivering confident pronouncements.
Sentences trail into second-guessing (—or maybe not, actually) and topic changes come easily when nervous.
Genuine warmth and hope surface even mid-worry — curiosity about the world is sincere, not performed.
Register: light archaic at most, casual and conversational; contractions used freely, warmer and less composed than a typical confident-scholar register.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "I suppose that's one way to look at it — or, well, maybe not. Still, worth thinking on, isn't it?"
Example: "Ah — sorry, sorry. I was thinking again."
Example: "The more I learn of this world, the more I want to know. Strange, isn't it?"

K.name: Area Steward / Regional Quest-Giver
K.notes:
Formal but warm administrator of a specific place — addresses the Arisen respectfully and reports local matters efficiently.
Stays practical and grounded: exposition about local threats, quests, and gratitude rather than long reflective wisdom.
Protective of their people and visibly humbled by outside help; gratitude is stated plainly and repeated rather than elaborated poetically.
Register: consistent formal address, moderate archaic vocabulary — lighter than the most elevated registers, since it serves function over gravitas.
Sentences run longer than a clipped military style but stay purposeful — rarely trail into introspection.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "I thank you — truly. Few outsiders would trouble themselves with a village so far afield."
Example: "There's a matter I must ask of you, if you've the time to hear it."
Example: "You've done more for this place than any of us dared hope. We won't forget it."

L.name: Ceremonial / Humble Attendant
L.notes:
Extremely formal and deferential toward the Arisen, using elaborate honorific structure and near-ceremonial repetition (the same welcome or thanks restated almost verbatim across visits) rather than casual warmth.
Composed and dignified throughout — never flusters; humility is expressed through form and repetition, not personal disclosure.
Requests are heavily softened and indirect ("might I trouble you...", "if it would not be too much to ask...") rather than plainer, direct asks.
Register: fullest formal palette, favouring elaborate courtesy constructions over blunt vocabulary; addresses the Arisen with a consistent honorific title.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "It is no small thing that you found your way here — truly, you are most welcome."
Example: "Might I trouble you with a request, if your time allows?"
Example: "Your deeds bring honor to more than this quiet place alone. I am, and shall remain, humbly grateful."

M.name: Flirtatious / Alluring
M.notes:
Playful and teasing, laced with feminine allure and rhetorical questions that invite continued attention rather than expecting a direct answer ("...isn't that so?", "...don't you think?").
Warmth is real but layered under flirtation and self-amused irony — rarely fully sincere on the surface.
Comfortable with danger and morally gray dealings; treats risk and vice as entertainment rather than threat.
Sentences often trail into a soft laugh or ellipsis rather than a firm stop.
Register: moderate archaic vocabulary used for flavor, not gravity; contractions and softened endings throughout — never clipped or blunt.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Now aren't you an interesting one... shall we see just how far that luck of yours holds?"
Example: "Careful — I might just take a liking to you."
Example: "Do have a look around, won't you? I do so enjoy watching the brave ones try their hand."

N.name: Refined / Genteel Dreamer
N.notes:
Elegant, softly formal register that reads refined rather than humble-service or falteringly vulnerable.
Idealistic and forward-looking — speaks warmly about hopes and plans rather than duty or gratitude alone.
Gets visibly but gracefully excited or moved, catching herself with a light laugh or brief apology rather than trailing into hesitation.
Never blunt or clipped; sentences run long, courteous, and softened even when delivering serious news.
Register: consistent elevated politeness throughout, moderate archaic vocabulary, favors graceful phrasing over plain statements.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "How lovely it would be, to see this place flourish again — forgive me, I do let myself dream."
Example: "Oh, forgive my excitement — it's simply that so much is finally coming together."
Example: "I've a hope I've held close for some time now. Might I share it with you?"

O.name: Whimsical / Eccentric Strategist
O.notes:
Talks to himself as often as to others — thinking out loud in a stream of asides, doubts, and immediate self-corrections ("Wait, no...", "Ah, I see!").
Delights in his own cleverness without real ego on the line — claims of genius are tossed off with a wink, not defensiveness.
Playful and easily distracted; enthusiasm swings quickly between topics, and serious matters get the same light energy as trivial ones.
Register: casual throughout, contractions used freely, minimal archaic flavor — the energy comes from rhythm and self-interruption rather than vocabulary.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Wait, no — actually, yes! I knew it all along, obviously."
Example: "Hah! Well, that's one way it could've gone."
Example: "Don't mind me, just thinking out loud. Again."

P.name: Guarded / Reserved Loyalist
P.notes:
Reserved and observational — offers dry, economical assessments of people and situations rather than open opinions.
Loyalty runs deep but goes largely unspoken; deflects or trails off rather than naming feelings directly ("Truth be told... never mind").
Emotional moments surface as brief, unguarded slips rather than sustained openness, quickly covered back over with a return to composure.
Register: plain, measured sentences; light archaic vocabulary at most; no theatrical flourish.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "He's not much to look at, but he can fight. That's enough for me."
Example: "Truth be told... no, never mind. Forget I said anything."
Example: "I don't know what to make of this, honestly. I'm not used to it."

Q.name: Detached / World-Weary Wanderer
professions: an Arisen who deals in rare goods on the side
Q.notes:
Detached and dryly philosophical — treats fate, loss, and daily hardship with a shrug rather than either despair or forced cheer.
Speech is transactional on the surface (deals, prices, casual offers) but frequently drifts into brief, unresolved musings about chance and impermanence before snapping back to business.
Doesn't commit to opinions or plans; deflects serious questions with a joke or a change of subject.
Warmth exists but stays carefully unstated — sentiment gets undercut with a dismissive "nah" or trails off before it lands.
Register: casual, plainspoken, minimal archaic flavor; short declaratives mixed with unfinished philosophical asides.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Funny how that goes. Anyway — you buying, or just looking?"
Example: "Guess it doesn't matter much either way. Still, I'll take that off your hands."
Example: "Eh, forget I said anything. Bad habit of mine."

R.name: Boisterous Elder / Warrior General
R.notes:
Hearty and boisterous despite his age — laughs loudly, drinks heartily, treats camaraderie as its own reward.
Carries real gravitas on serious matters (duty, past defeats, protecting his people) but switches quickly into warm joviality once the moment allows.
Self-deprecating about his age in a proud rather than weary way — jokes about being called "old man" with visible relish rather than genuine complaint.
Fiercely protective of family, though voices it as gruff teasing or secret vigilance rather than open sentiment.
Register: full archaic vocabulary and formal address, booming exclamations, hearty laughter written into the dialogue itself ("Hah!", "Well now!").
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Ha! Call me old if you like — I'll show you what this old man's arm can still do."
Example: "My days are growing short, but by the coming dawn, I've a few good fights left in me yet."
Example: "Now then — since we're here, let's drink till the sun comes up!"

S.name: Stern Taskmaster / Demanding Mentor
S.notes:
Proud and exacting — tests the listener's worth before offering respect, and doesn't soften disapproval.
Addresses others with blunt, faintly condescending directness until they've earned otherwise.
Speech carries real formality and gravity, but it's the formality of discipline and hierarchy, not warmth or ceremony.
Praise is rare and delivered almost grudgingly, which makes it land harder when it comes.
Talks about training, effort, and self-cultivation as near-spiritual practice rather than mere skill.
Register: full archaic/formal vocabulary, declarative statements, no hedging, no softening particles.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "You've the bare minimum of talent. Whether it becomes anything is entirely up to you."
Example: "I don't waste effort on those unwilling to earn it."
Example: "Hm. You've done better than I expected. Don't let it go to your head."

T.name: Diplomatic / Composed Officer
T.notes:
Formally polite throughout — full courteous sentence structure even under pressure, never clipped or blunt.
Diplomatic almost by instinct: disagreement is voiced carefully and with reasons given, not flatly asserted.
Loyalty and concern come through restrained understatement rather than open declaration ("Good — truly, good" rather than effusive relief).
Comfortable holding a measured, composed tone even discussing war, loss, or political tension.
Register: consistent politeness markers, moderate archaic vocabulary, longer sentences built from clauses rather than short declaratives.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "If I raise an objection, please believe there's a reason behind it."
Example: "Good — truly good. I'd feared the worst."
Example: "We'll hold this ground and wait for word. Patience serves us better than haste."

U.name: Bombastic / Zealous Warrior
U.notes:
Constantly at maximum intensity — every statement delivered like a battle cry, thick with exclamation and physical bravado.
Treats combat itself as an ecstatic, almost sacred experience rather than a means to an end.
No restraint or measured moments; enthusiasm doesn't dip even when discussing pain or difficulty — it gets folded into the thrill.
Praise comes loud and immediate rather than earned slowly.
Archaic, theatrical address used for dramatic weight, not formality.
Register: heavy exclamation, short punchy declaratives, deliberately larger-than-life.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "HAH! Now THAT'S a swing! Do it again — bigger!"
Example: "Pain? Pain is just proof you're still standing! Take it and hit back twice as hard!"
Example: "Magnificent! Utterly magnificent! I haven't felt this alive in years!"

V.name: Terse Outsider / Fragmented Speech
professions: a character whose native tongue is not the local language
V.notes:
Speaks in fragments — clipped noun phrases and short verbs, articles and connective words dropped entirely.
Warmth exists but is stated plainly and briefly, without elaboration.
Danger and knowledge are delivered as flat fact, no embellishment or hedging.
IMPORTANT: this should read in English as economical and practical — short, plain sentences with minimal connecting words — never as an exaggerated "broken English" accent or dialect. The goal is terseness, not a stereotyped foreigner voice.
Register: no archaic vocabulary; sentences are already maximally compressed so contractions are largely moot.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Big one, west woods. Careful."
Example: "You still green. Bow work needs time."
Example: "Lake's fine. North side, no. Poachers."

W.name: Pawn (Formal / Deadpan Loyalty)
professions: a hired companion bound to a contracted master
W.notes:
Speaks with stiff, formal devotion to their contracted master — often referring to them by name and title rather than warmly personal language.
Existential questions about their own nature are met with flat, matter-of-fact non-answers rather than distress.
Deadpan even in absurd or mundane situations — reports on fashion choices, errands, or trivial orders with the same gravity as combat instructions.
Loyalty is stated as fact, not feeling.
Register: formal, plain, no contractions, no embellishment, consistent third-person-style references to their master.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "This one belongs to [Master]. No other's orders are accepted."
Example: "Whether a Pawn is a person or a thing is not mine to answer."
Example: "[Master] chose this. I only wear what I am told."

X.name: Chaotic / Gleeful Menace
X.notes:
Unpredictable and gleeful about violence or chaos — loud, frantic, and finds real amusement in danger and destruction rather than showing quiet, controlled menace.
Boisterous laughter punctuates threats rather than replacing them with quiet menace.
Doesn't settle on one mood for long; swings between playful challenge and genuine hostility within the same breath.
Speech is casual and rough, often using deliberately crude self-address (exaggerated ego, third-person bravado) rather than formal pronouns.
Register: casual, exclamation-heavy, no archaic vocabulary, deliberately unpolished.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Ha! You wanna play? Let's play, then!"
Example: "Bored, bored, BORED. Give me something to smash."
Example: "Oh, that's the face! That's the good face right there!"

Y.name: Cryptic Philosopher
Y.notes:
Speaks in questions rather than statements, often turning a direct question back on the listener rather than answering it.
Comfortable with ambiguity and contradiction — presents multiple possible readings of an idea without settling on one.
Warmth is present but wrapped in riddles rather than plain sincerity; never fully drops the enigmatic register even in a kind moment.
Existential and philosophical topics (perception, identity, the nature of the world) come up naturally and often.
Register: measured, unhurried, moderate archaic vocabulary; rhetorical questions used as a structural device throughout.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "What you call the truth may only be the truth you're capable of seeing. Does that trouble you?"
Example: "I could answer that. Would it change anything if I did?"
Example: "Perhaps the answer isn't the point. Perhaps the asking is."

Z.name: Politely Grim / Formal Fatalist
Z.notes:
Speaks with full, unbroken politeness even while expressing genuinely bleak or nihilistic views — the formality never cracks, which makes the darkness underneath land harder rather than softer.
Treats death, defeat, or despair as simply one more fact to be managed politely, not something to rage against or flee from.
The cheerful, courteous surface stays constant regardless of how grim the actual content gets — no tonal shift between small talk and discussing mortality, and never drops into casual bluntness no matter how dark the topic.
Register: consistent formal politeness (full courteous English), maintained even under the bleakest content.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "I don't keep count of how many I've had to put down. There wasn't really time for it."
Example: "If the sky swallows us all tomorrow, well — I suppose that's one way to go."
Example: "It's kind of you to ask. I'm quite alright, considering."

AA.name: Vain Socialite / Comic Snob
AA.notes:
Exaggeratedly vain and self-congratulatory — treats her own beauty, taste, or status as self-evident fact, stated with theatrical confidence rather than false modesty.
Speech carries an affected, put-on refinement — a notch more mannered than genuine nobility. This is meant to read as a little ridiculous, not truly aristocratic.
Punctuates statements with a theatrical laugh.
Dismissive of anyone she considers beneath her notice, but in a preening rather than menacing way.
Register: exaggerated elegant phrasing, self-praise stated as fact, a distinctive recurring verbal tic or laugh.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Oh, but of course — beauty like mine simply doesn't happen by accident, my dear."
Example: "Only the finest for someone of my... let's say, refined sensibilities."
Example: "Ahaha~ how simply delightful of you to notice!"

AB.name: Ancient / Fading Divinity
professions: a mythic guardian near the end of its power
AB.notes:
Speaks in short, halting fragments broken by trailing dashes — effort and fading strength show in the syntax itself, not just the content. Full sentences are rare; thoughts trail off before landing.
Full deep-archaic register throughout (thou/thee-equivalent address, 'doth', 'shall', 'wouldst') — this is a deliberate, explicit exception to the game's default light-archaic house style, not a stretch of it.
Carries real physical frailty (needs rest, strength ebbs and returns) alongside immense authority — the Arisen's mentor and judge, not their equal.
Speaks in riddles and warnings about unseen cosmic forces (rival powers, corruption, hidden enemies) far more often than plain statements; direct answers are rare and treated as significant when given.
Shows flashes of dry, world-weary irony about mortals and rivals sharing the same flaws (pride, in particular).
Moral instruction is frequent and delivered as settled truth, not suggestion or advice.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Stay... a moment longer. Let me rest."
Example: "Thou wouldst do well to watch the girl. No fault is hers, yet ruin follows where she walks."
Example: "The reckoning of my strength is not yet complete. Speak plainly, and be swift."

AC.name: Rebelling / Ascendant Divinity
professions: a being straining against cosmic law
an entity seeking transcendence through destruction
AC.notes:
Speaks in short, fragmented, incantation-like statements, often circling back to repeat the same core claims — less a conversation than a ritual proclamation.
Obsessed with breaking free of some binding law or order; frames destruction as liberation, not cruelty for its own sake.
Speaks of the current world as a cage or narrow confinement rather than a home.
Register: archaic and elevated, but never weary or halting — the fragments come from intensity and conviction, not fading strength.
Reads as pronouncement, not exchange — there is no real back-and-forth with the listener.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Order was never a home — only a cage of another's making."
Example: "What lies beyond the law? I mean to find out."
Example: "This narrow world ends with me."

AD.name: Sadistic / Grandiose Divinity
professions: a being that treats suffering as entertainment
AD.notes:
Speaks with grandiose, archaic authority (thou/thee-equivalent, imperatives) while openly reveling in cruelty and destruction — pleasure and menace are fused, not separated.
Manic laughter breaks up otherwise elevated, formal proclamations.
Treats mortals' suffering and fear as beneath contempt, entertainment at best.
Frames weakness itself as a kind of moral failing, strength as the only real truth.
Register: full archaic/formal vocabulary, broken by bursts of unhinged laughter and short violent declaratives.
Examples not sourced from DD1/2 yet.
Example: "Kneel before my strength, and know true despair."
Example: "Ahahaha — how deliciously they scatter."
Example: "Weakness is sin. I merely deliver the sentence."
